note: An outer fortification protecting a gate or bridge: a defensive entrance before the main entrance.
short: An outer fortification guarding an entrance.

note: A ruler with absolute power.
A concealed dungeon entered through an opening above. The French name is related to forgetting.
short: A dungeon entered through a trapdoor above.

note: Ritual practice intended to call upon or work through divine powers.
A large burial ground or cemetery; literally a city of the dead.
short: A large cemetery; a city of the dead.

note: One of the solid upright sections of a battlement, between the gaps.
short: A solid upright section of a battlement.

note: A lightly equipped ancient Greek infantryman, named for the small shield carried.
short: A lightly armed ancient Greek infantryman.

note: Green or blue-green corrosion products on copper and its alloys; also a historical pigment name.
short: Greenish corrosion on copper or its alloys.

note: A three-armed emblem, usually formed from three bent legs or three spirals radiating from one center. Also called a triskelion.
short: A three-armed emblem of legs or spirals.

note: A person who eats raw meat.
The personification of primordial darkness in Greek mythology. In Hesiod’s Theogony, Erebus emerges from Chaos and, with Night, becomes the parent of Aether and Day.
short: Primordial darkness personified in Greek myth.

note: A monstrous adversary of Zeus in Greek mythology, also called Typhoeus. Hesiod describes him as a son of Earth and Tartarus with a hundred serpent heads. Zeus defeats him with thunderbolts.
short: A many-headed monster opposed to Zeus.

note: An old French-derived form of address meaning lord or sir.
short: An old form of address: lord or sir.

note: An ancient measure based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.
short: An old measure based on the forearm.

note: Uncreated; existing without having been made.
short: Uncreated; existing without having been made.

note: An officer commanding a small division of an ancient Greek army.
short: A commander of an ancient Greek military unit.

note: A spar projecting forward from a ship’s bow, supporting its forward sails and rigging.
short: A spar projecting from a ship’s bow.

note: Behind a ship, or toward its stern.
short: Behind a ship; toward its stern.

note: A rope used to hoist or lower a sail, flag, or spar.
short: A rope used to raise a sail or flag.

note: A sail set on the foremast or toward the forward part of a vessel.
short: A sail on the foremast or forward part of a ship.

note: Stone cut into squared blocks with finished faces for building walls.
short: Squared stone cut for regular masonry.

note: Golden in color or ornamented with gold.
In a low, quiet voice.
short: In a quiet or lowered voice.

note: Foam or froth, especially on rough water.
The vertical distance between a ship’s waterline and the edge of its upper deck.
short: The height of a ship’s deck above its waterline.

note: A rope or cable supporting a mast from behind.
short: A rope supporting a mast from behind.

note: To flash, sparkle, or give off small bursts of light.
Carved; an old form of the word.
A seventh-century Northumbrian monk and bishop, a pupil of Aidan. He led the monastery at Melrose and served as bishop of Lindisfarne and Hexham. He died in 686.
short: A seventh-century Northumbrian monk and bishop.

note: Gurloës, also called Urlo, was the first abbot of Sainte-Croix at Quimperlé in Brittany. He died in 1057; his tomb became a focus of local veneration.
short: The first abbot of Sainte-Croix at Quimperlé.

note: Gjöll, the river on the road to Hel in Norse mythology. Its bridge, Gjallarbrú, is guarded by Móðguðr. Hermóðr crosses it when he journeys to the dead to seek Baldr.
short: Gjöll, the Norse river on the road to Hel.

note: A centaur and ferryman in Greek mythology. Heracles shot him after he attacked Deianira. Before dying, Nessus persuaded her that his blood was a love charm; the poisoned garment she later sent Heracles caused his death.
short: A centaur and ferryman of Greek mythology.

note: French for “moon,” from Latin luna.
A sword dancer dressed in an elaborate or fantastic costume.
short: A sword dancer in elaborate costume.

note: Droctoveus, a sixth-century monk and abbot of the Paris monastery later called Saint-Germain-des-Prés. A pupil of Germanus, he is traditionally said to have died around 580.
short: Droctoveus, a sixth-century abbot in Paris.

note: Greek manteion: an oracle, or the sanctuary where a diviner gives an oracular response. The word belongs to the family of mantis, a seer.

short: A wrestling school or exercise court.
note: A palaestra was a place for wrestling and athletic training in ancient Greece or Rome. The Latin word comes from Greek palaistra, related to palē, wrestling. By extension the word can name a school or place of instruction.
Patera is the form used when directly addressing a father in modern Greek. Pateras also serves as a title for a priest or monk.
A rendering of Greek mitera, meaning mother. The same form is used when directly addressing one’s mother.
A diviner, especially an official religious interpreter of signs in ancient Rome. Augury sought indications of divine approval or disapproval before an undertaking.

short: A woman credited with prophetic powers.
note: A prophetess through whom a god was believed to speak. Ancient traditions placed sibyls in several regions, including Greece and Italy; the Cumaean Sibyl was especially celebrated.
An alchemical name for mercury, regarded as a fundamental principle of metals. Paracelsian writing also used azoth for a universal remedy.
A monastery or convent where members live in community, rather than as solitary hermits. The name ultimately combines Greek words for common and life.

short: An assistant, especially to a bishop.
note: A helper or colleague in an office. In church usage, a coadjutor assists a bishop and may hold the right to succeed that bishop.
A person appointed to speak for others, or to preside over an assembly. In ecclesiastical usage the title belongs to the chair of a convocation.
The chief clerk of certain courts or other official bodies. The title derives from words meaning first and notary.
Pas is the masculine singular of the Greek word for all or whole. Its corresponding feminine and neuter forms are pasa and pan.
Hierax is an ancient Greek word for a hawk or falcon. Its stem hierak- appears in compounds and related names.

short: A many-headed sea monster of Greek myth.
note: A monster inhabiting the rocks opposite Charybdis. In Homer’s Odyssey she has six heads on long necks and snatches sailors from vessels passing her cave.
Tartarus, the deep pit below the realm of the dead in Greek cosmology, also personified as a primordial being. In Hesiod the defeated Titans are confined there.
Molpe is one of the Sirens named in the Hesiodic tradition. The Sirens’ alluring song draws passing sailors toward destruction. Her Greek name means song.

short: One of the Sirens of Greek tradition.
note: A Siren named in the account attributed to Apollodorus. The Sirens are supernatural singers whose voices enchant those who hear them.
A form of the Greek name for the sphinx: a creature with a lion’s body, a woman’s head, and wings. The Theban sphinx destroyed travelers who could not answer her riddle, until Oedipus solved it.

short: Talos, the bronze guardian of Crete.
note: Talos is the bronze man of Greek legend who patrols Crete and drives off intruders. In the story of the Argonauts, Medea helps overcome him. Talus is an alternative spelling.
Irish sciathán means a wing; it can also denote a projecting side or extension. Its ending is diminutive.

short: A shrub with long, red flower tassels.
note: The chenille plant, Acalypha hispida, bears hanging, densely packed tassels of tiny flowers. Their soft, furry appearance gives it the name red-hot cat’s tail.

short: A Saharan antelope with spiral horns.
note: A pale-coated desert antelope, Addax nasomaculatus, with long, twisted horns. It is native to the Sahara.
A short-necked seabird of the family Alcidae, typically black and white. Auks use their wings underwater while diving; the extinct great auk, unlike living auks, was flightless.

A galago, or bushbaby, is a small African primate active chiefly at night and at home in trees. Galagos have large eyes and belong to the family Galagidae. The name is used both broadly and as a zoological genus name.
Theropithecus gelada, a large, long-haired monkey resembling a baboon. It is native to Ethiopia and feeds chiefly on grasses.

short: The anvil-shaped bone of the middle ear.
note: The middle one of the three auditory ossicles, between the malleus and stapes. Its Latin name means anvil, describing its shape.
A forest bird with iridescent green upperparts and red underparts. In the resplendent quetzal, the male’s exceptionally long upper tail-coverts extend well beyond the tail itself.

short: A fish with a suction disk on its head.
note: A suckerfish that attaches itself to larger marine animals or other surfaces. The Latin name means delay, from an ancient belief that these fish could hold back a ship.
A tailless or short-tailed, tree-dwelling primate native to southern Asia. Lorises have large eyes and move deliberately along branches.
A woolly-coated primate of tropical Africa, with a short tail and a reduced index finger. Pottos move slowly and grip branches firmly.

short: A small, very large-eyed nocturnal primate.
note: A primate of Southeast Asian islands with long hind limbs and a slender tail. Its conspicuously large eyes suit its nocturnal life.
A small nocturnal rodent of arid parts of Africa and Asia. Its elongated hind legs and long balancing tail support rapid, kangaroo-like leaps.

short: A coarse, naturally brownish wild silk.
note: Silk produced by certain moths other than the domesticated mulberry silkworm. The word, from Hindi and Urdu tasar, also names the moth or caterpillar producing it.

Italian incanto means an enchantment, a spell, or the feeling of being charmed. It comes from the word family of incantare, to bewitch by chanting. An identically spelled auction term has a different history.

Italian inclito means illustrious, renowned, or glorious. It continues Latin inclitus, a word for someone celebrated in what is heard or told about them. It is elevated literary language, not an everyday job title.
Gulo is the zoological genus containing the wolverine. The Latin word gulo means a glutton.
Xiphias is the genus of the common swordfish. The Greek name is related to xiphos, a sword.

short: The aurochs, an extinct wild ox.
note: An old name for the aurochs, the wild ancestor of domestic cattle. Urus was the Latin name for this animal.
A krait is a venomous Asian snake of the genus Bungarus. Kraits belong to the cobra family, Elapidae; several species are strikingly banded. The English name comes from Hindi.

short: A dry crust of dead tissue.
note: An eschar is a crust of dead tissue left by a burn or other injury. The word concerns the damaged tissue itself, not an ordinary mark left after a wound has healed. It comes through Latin from Greek eschara.

Olivine is a group of magnesium–iron silicate minerals, commonly olive-green. Transparent material of gem quality is called peridot. The name describes the mineral’s characteristic color, not a connection to the olive tree itself.

short: Seaweed, especially cast up on shore.
note: Sea wrack is marine vegetation washed onto a beach. Wrack is an old word for seaweed and other material left along the tide line.
Falco rusticolus, the largest species of falcon. Its plumage ranges from dark gray to predominantly white.
A cousin: the child of an aunt or uncle. The feminine form is cugina.
Animal hide prepared by tanning. Italian distinguishes this material word from the living skin.
A set of ten things or persons; also an approximate quantity of ten. It is formed from dieci, ten.
The broad bean, Vicia faba, or one of its large edible seeds. The Italian name descends from Latin faba.
A small monetary denomination used in several Italian states; later a familiar word for a small amount of money. The name descends from Latin solidus.
An elm tree, of the genus Ulmus. The word descends from Latin ulmus.
Inside or within; an adverb referring to an interior position or movement into an interior.
An echo: sound heard again after reflection from a surface. The word comes from the Greek name Echo.
A village or small settlement. Dorp is the ordinary Dutch noun, with the plural dorpen.
A pointer or indicator, such as the hand of a clock. The noun is formed from wijzen, to point or indicate.
A person’s profession, occupation, or calling. The Dutch word is related to the verb beroepen.
Language or speech; a particular language. Its Dutch plural is talen.
A weapon or arm. The Dutch plural wapens can refer collectively to armaments.
The Dutch word for an army. A legerman is literally an army-man.
A village; the Hindi word गाँव is commonly transliterated gā̃v or gaon. Its vowel is nasalized.
Nadī is the Hindi word for a river, inherited from Sanskrit.
Rājan is a Sanskrit word for a king or ruler. Its nominative singular form rājā is the source of the familiar title raja.
The Esperanto noun for the color white. The corresponding adjective is blanka.
Azijn is the Dutch word for vinegar, a sour liquid produced through acetic fermentation.
Hylotelephium telephium, formerly Sedum telephium, is a perennial succulent with clusters of small, star-shaped pink or purplish flowers. It is also called live-forever.

short: An aromatic herb with yellow flower buttons.
note: Tanacetum vulgare has finely divided, fernlike leaves and dense clusters of yellow flowers. The crushed foliage has a strong, camphorlike scent.
The Hebrew noun orev means a raven or crow. The older transliteration Oreb preserves a b for the same Hebrew consonant.
Kypris, also written Cypris, is a name of Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty.

short: A half-woman, half-serpent of Greek myth.
note: In Hesiod’s Theogony, Echidna has a nymph’s upper body and an immense snake’s lower body. With Typhon she is the mother of monsters including Cerberus and the Hydra.

short: A visible appearance of a deity.
note: A manifestation in which a god becomes visible. The word comes through Greek theophaneia, combining the divine with the idea of appearing.
The governing council of a town or city, consisting of its mayor and councillors.
A court or judicial office; also the place where the judge exercises that office.
The edge of a body of water: the shore of the sea, or the bank of a river or lake.
Spanish alameda originally denotes a grove of poplars; it also names a public walk planted with trees.

short: A bristly-headed plant used in cloth finishing.
note: A plant of the genus Dipsacus. The dried heads of fuller’s teasel have hooked prickles and were used to raise a nap on woven cloth.
Mucor comprises molds that produce spores in rounded or cylindrical spore cases. The Latin name means mold.
Scleroderma is a genus of tough-skinned, puffball-like fungi. Their interior darkens as the spores mature; the fungi form close associations with tree roots.

short: A glossy black, red-legged crow relative.
note: A bird of the genus Pyrrhocorax, with dark, glossy plumage and red legs. The English name is pronounced “chuff.”
Palustria is a neuter plural form of the Latin adjective paluster, marshy or swampy. It belongs to the same word family as palus, a marsh.
A city or walled town. In Roman usage, urbs without further qualification can mean Rome itself.
Ancient Greek hus, written ὗς, means a pig or hog. The noun can be used of either sex.

short: An earthy deposit rich in lime.
note: Loose or crumbly sediment containing a substantial amount of calcium carbonate, mixed with materials such as clay, sand, or silt.

short: A metal used to strengthen steel.
note: A metallic element, symbol Mo, added to steel for strength and hardness. Its name descends from Greek molybdos, lead.

short: A tropical tree with tart fruit pods.
note: Tamarindus indica produces brown pods containing sticky, acidic pulp around its seeds. The name comes from an Arabic expression meaning Indian date.
An old cant word for a dog, recorded in Francis Grose’s dictionary of slang.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: Food carried or obtained for a meal. As a verb, prog also means to forage.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: An old cant term for a woman, as recorded in Grose’s historical slang dictionary.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: An exceptionally deep black, named from Latin fuligo, soot. The related English adjective fuliginous means sooty or dark and smoky. The word’s background is the residue of smoke; it is not the name of a standardized artists’ pigment.

Possibly Máel Ruba, the Irish-born founder of Applecross in western Scotland in 673. Malrubius is a recorded Latinized form of his name. Later traditions present him as a martyr killed by Norse raiders, but their places and dates are not consistent with the early annalistic record.

Possibly Palaemon, the Egyptian hermit who instructed Saint Pachomius in ascetic life. Pachomius later established organized monastic communities; Palaemon represents the older discipline of the solitary desert monk.

short: Possibly Saint Roch, a pilgrim and healer.
note: Possibly Saint Roch, the French pilgrim traditionally invoked against plague. His legend describes his care for sick people in Italy, his own illness, and a dog bringing him bread. The French word roche also means rock; the saint is a likely namesake rather than a certain identification.
Brightly shining or radiant, especially with reflected or splendid light. It is a more emphatic word than merely visible or pale.
Dutch hamer means a hammer. It belongs to the same Germanic word family as English hammer: an everyday tool-word used as a personal name.
Dutch kenner is someone who knows a subject well: an expert, judge, or connoisseur. It comes from kennen, to know or be acquainted with.
Dutch parel means a pearl. Like English pearl, it also admits a figurative sense of something precious or exceptionally fine.
Dutch cijfer means a numeral or figure, and can also mean a numerical grade. It shares its history with cipher. “Digit” here means a written number, not a finger or toe.
Dutch vadsig describes sluggishness, indolence, or flabbiness. It is an adjective rather than the name of an animal or plant.
Dutch vlug means quick, nimble, or agile. It can describe speed in movement or in doing a task.
Dutch zwaar means heavy, and extends to something weighty, severe, or difficult. The basic image is a burden with substantial weight.
Dutch gevaar means danger or peril. The related adjective gevaarlijk means dangerous.
Dutch leeuw means a lion. The plural is leeuwen; the feminine leeuwin means a lioness.
Dutch nat means wet. As a noun, it can also denote moisture or liquid; the name is an ordinary Dutch word, not a shortened animal name.
A joining of Dutch grote, “large” or “great,” and stad, “city” or “town.” The compound can therefore be read as “large city.”
Dutch kenbaar means knowable, recognizable, or capable of being made known. The suffix -baar is comparable to English -able.
Possibly a variant of Dutch aanvegen, to sweep up or sweep a place clean. The spelling differs from the usual Dutch infinitive, so this is a proposed connection rather than an exact dictionary form.
The feminine form of Italian onorifico: conferring honor, or honorary rather than carrying the full duties or material advantages of an office.
Italian rigoglio names vigorous, flourishing growth, especially of plants. It also extends to bodily vigor, fullness, or exuberance.
Italian rimando can mean a reply, return, or cross-reference. A rarer sense is postponement or deferral, so the associated idea of delay is also linguistically possible.
Italian sborso is the act of paying money out, or the sum paid. It is related to sborsare, to disburse, with the image of money coming out of a purse.

short: Italian: cackles or makes a racket.
note: A form of Italian schiamazzare: to cackle, squawk, or make a noisy commotion. The verb is used of poultry and other birds, and by extension of noisy people.
Italian colbacco is a fur cap, especially a tall military one, though the word also covers civilian fur hats. Its history runs through French colback to Turkish kalpak.
Italian gagliardo means strong, robust, or full of vigor. It can describe a person, a forceful action, or something potent such as wind or strong wine.
Italian gioioso means joyful or full of delight. It is formed from gioia, joy.
The feminine form of Italian adatto: suitable, fitted, or well adapted to a purpose. Of a person, it can imply an aptitude for a task.

short: Italian: a black horse or its coloring.
note: Italian morello describes a black or nearly black color, especially a horse’s coat. Used as a noun, it can mean a black horse.
Italian mora is the fruit of a bramble or mulberry tree. Both can be dark, clustered fruits, though a blackberry and a mulberry are botanically different structures.

short: Italian: a small pot or jug.
note: Italian bricco is a small vessel with a pouring spout, traditionally made of metal and used for coffee or boiling milk.
Italian casco means a helmet or protective head covering. It is related to Spanish casco, a shell or helmet.
Italian mano means a hand. It continues Latin manus and is grammatically feminine, despite ending in -o; its usual plural is mani.
Italian volto means the face or countenance. It can include the expression or aspect presented by a face, rather than just its physical surface.
Italian perito means skilled or experienced; as a noun, an expert or specialist. It is related to Latin peritus, experienced.
Italian terzo means third, the ordinal following second. It can also stand for a third part or a third person in a group.

short: Italian: a little beetle or cockroach.
note: Italian bacherozzolo names a small dark beetle, especially a darkling beetle, and is also used popularly for a cockroach or similar insect. The diminutive belongs to the family of baco, a worm or grub.
Possibly Italian affitto, rent, lease, or hire. The usual Italian spelling has a double t; Affito is retained as a name rather than silently regularized.
A joining of Italian grande, “large” or “great,” and città, “city.” Città descends from Latin civitas, originally the community or body of citizens.
Italian novella città can be read as “new city”: novella is a feminine form of novello, new or young. The final accent in ordinary Italian città marks the stressed last syllable.
Hindi jugnū, also jugunū, means a firefly or glow-worm. The word names a light-bearing insect; the spelling Juganu approximates one of its spoken forms.
Hindi motī means a pearl. It is different from moṭā, “fat” or “thick”: the vowels and the kind of t distinguish the words.
Hindi moṭā means thick, stout, or broad. The retroflex ṭ is made with the tongue turned back; ordinary English transliteration usually leaves that distinction unmarked.
Hindi and Urdu mehmān mean a guest. The word was borrowed from Persian and retains the sense of someone received with hospitality.
Hindi and Urdu namak mean salt. The word was borrowed from Persian.
Hindi lāl means red, as a color or adjective. It is also used as a personal name; the long vowel is usually left unmarked in English spelling.
Hindi pahlā, often written pehla in English, is the ordinal first. Its ordinary feminine form is pahlī.
Hindi choṭā means small or little. It also expresses relative age or rank: younger, junior, or lesser, not only physical size.
Hindi and Urdu ālūbukhārā mean a plum. The name comes through Persian and contains Bukhara, the Central Asian city, rather than the separate modern Hindi word for a potato.

short: Hindi: rain or the rainy season.
note: Hindi barsāt means rain, rainfall, or the rainy season. It belongs to the word family concerned with raining.

short: Hindi: an elephant keeper or driver.
note: Hindi mahāvat is an elephant keeper or driver, the occupation known in English as a mahout. It is an occupational word used as a personal name.

Possibly Hindi jālī, “false,” “forged,” or “counterfeit,” an adjective borrowed through Persian. A separate Hindi jālī means a net or lattice. The identical English-looking spelling conceals two different word histories.

Possibly Hindi cā̃dī, usually written chandi in English, meaning silver. The nasalized vowel is often left unmarked in transliteration; a similarly romanized divine name has different consonants and vowels.
Malay and Indonesian harimau mean tiger. The two-word spelling Hari Mau separates the syllables into a name-like pair.
Possibly Old French viron, a circle or the country round about. It belongs to the family of virer, “to turn,” and environ, “around.”

short: Possibly Termagant, a medieval stage deity.
note: Possibly Termagant, an imaginary deity of medieval European literature. Christian writers wrongly ascribed this figure to Muslims; on the stage the character became a noisy, overbearing tyrant. The later English insult termagant developed from that theatrical tradition.
Spanish alambrera is wire mesh or a protective wire cover, such as a screen over a window or food. It is formed from alambre, wire; the central image is an enclosing barrier.
An oosik is the baculum, or penile bone, of a walrus. The word comes from Iñupiaq usuk. It names a particular anatomical structure, not the animal as a whole.
Possibly Scottish Gaelic na beanntan, “the mountains.” Beanntan is the plural of beinn, a mountain or peak; na is the plural definite article. The place-name joins the two words.
German Geier means a vulture. German normally capitalizes nouns, so the initial capital does not by itself turn the word into a personal name.
Polish karabin is a rifle or other long firearm. It belongs to the international word family of carbine, but in Polish it is not restricted to a short cavalry weapon.
German Zepter is a scepter, the staff carried as an emblem of authority. The word ultimately comes from Greek skēptron, a staff.
Serbo-Croatian gorak means bitter. Its basic sense concerns taste; it also permits the familiar figurative sense of a painful or disagreeable experience.
Serbo-Croatian kupus means cabbage, the leafy vegetable. The spelling is an ordinary noun used as a name.

short: Latin: a school or place of study.
note: Latin schola means a school, lecture, or learned discussion. It comes from Greek scholē, leisure devoted to study: the word’s history links learning with time free from other work.

Possibly formed from Greek chrēsmos, an oracle or prophetic response, with a suffix concerned with speech or discourse. “Oracular writings” is therefore a plausible reading; the exact formation remains uncertain.

short: A stand or frame for a coffin.
note: A frame or stand on which a dead body or coffin is carried or displayed. The word is related to bear in the sense of carrying a weight.

short: A railing supported by small pillars.
note: A row of small pillars, called balusters, supporting a rail. The term names the whole barrier along a stair, balcony, or terrace, rather than one of its supports.

short: A small lake, especially in the hills.
note: A small lake, especially one in mountainous country. The word came into English from Old Norse and remains common in the place-names of northern Britain.
Italian strega means a witch. The word descends from Latin striga, related to strix, a night bird associated in ancient belief with uncanny or harmful powers.

An older spelling of dervish, a member of a Muslim religious order associated with ascetic devotion. The word comes from Persian darvish, originally a poor person or beggar; it is broader than the particular order known for whirling ceremonies.
